US says it opposes Chinese 'coercion', after Belize and Paraguay ministers sanctioned

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said in response that the United States should "stop sending the wrong signals to Taiwan separatist forces".

Paraguay President Santiago Pena attends a welcoming ceremony with Taiwan leader Lai Ching-te in Taipei, Taiwan, on May 8, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Ann Wang)

TAIPEI: The Trump administration opposes "coercion and aggression" by China against countries for exercising their sovereign rights, the US State Department said, after Beijing sanctioned Belizean and Paraguayan ministers over their ties to Taiwan. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said in response that the United States should "stop sending the wrong signals to Taiwan separatist forces". Paraguay and Belize are two of just 12 countries to maintain formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan. China says Taiwan is one of its provinces with no right to behave like a state, a view Taipei's government strongly rejects. The sanctions are largely symbolic because ministers from Taiwan's diplomatic allies generally do not travel to China. Beijing has previously imposed similar measures mainly on Western politicians for their support of democratically governed Taiwan.

"The Trump administration opposes coercion and aggression by China against countries in our hemisphere for exercising their sovereign rights," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement. Pigott cited previous comments by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that the US "will not allow our region to become a base of operation for adversaries, competitors, and rivals to threaten our security or undermine our partnerships". "We stand with our friends and partners, including Taiwan, to advance our shared prosperity, security, and values," Pigott added. The United States is Taiwan's most important international backer, despite the lack of formal diplomatic ties. Washington has been concerned not only by Beijing's efforts to win over Taiwan's remaining allies, but also by attempts to increase its influence in Latin America.

Related:

TAIWAN'S VISIBILITY "GROWING HIGHER" Speaking on Tuesday (Oct 13) to reporters at parliament in Taipei, Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi said China was extending "transnational repression" to Taiwan's allies. "Taiwan's international visibility is growing higher and higher, and they will be kept busy by this fact," Chen said, referring to China. "Do they plan to sanction the whole world?" Taiwan Premier Cho Jung-tai said Beijing had no right to interfere in the domestic affairs of, or influence the diplomacy of, any sovereign and independent state, "including the Republic of China", referring to the island's formal name. "At the same time, we will resist any expansion of hegemony or authoritarianism," he added, also speaking at parliament. China has stepped up pressure on Taiwan's remaining diplomatic allies to sever ties with Taipei. The last country to do so was the tiny Pacific Island nation of Nauru, in 2024. Honduras ended its decades-long ties with Taiwan in 2023.

Source: Reuters/ec

SEOUL: South Korea's ambassador to the United States said Washington had raised concerns about intelligence cooperation between the allies and that Seoul had not yet fully addressed US expectations, Yonhap news agency reported on Tuesday (Oct 13). Ambassador Kang Kyung-wha told a South Korean parliamentary audit in Washington that intelligence sharing was the most difficult issue in bilateral relations, according to Yonhap. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio raised the matter during talks with South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun last month, Kang said. Kang did not detail Washington's concerns, but said communication between the two countries' intelligence agencies was continuing and had made progress.

The ambassador also said access to senior White House officials had been limited, according to the report. South Korea's foreign ministry did not immediately have a response to a Reuters request for comment on the report. South Korean media have reported that Washington asked that Seoul's National Intelligence Service be excluded from a June meeting with US and Japanese officials on North Korean cyber threats. Seoul's spy agency said the matter reflected a past misunderstanding and had been resolved, acknowledging restrictions on some intelligence connected to the earlier dispute but denying reports that the US had reduced sharing of North Korean missile information or cut the overall flow of intelligence. Kang said Seoul and Washington were discussing ways to secure South Korean rights to enrich uranium and reprocess spent nuclear fuel, either through revising their civil nuclear agreement or an additional arrangement. No progress had been made towards a summit between US President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, despite Trump signalling openness to dialogue, Kang said. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung told a cabinet meeting on Tuesday that Seoul should avoid subservient attitudes in dealings with other countries. Lee called the US alliance a central pillar of South Korean diplomacy which should be further developed, while adding that differences between countries were inevitable and should be managed through discussion and coordination.

AI investment props up global growth, but war and debt threaten outlook, IMF says

The IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1 per cent, a slight uptick from the 3.0 per cent it predicted in July.

BANGKOK: The global economy will still manage to top 3 per cent real GDP growth this year as strong AI investment offsets the energy shock from the war in the Middle East, but downside risks are mounting and more countries are being left behind and vulnerable to rising debt loads, the International Monetary Fund said on Tuesday. Despite a more protracted conflict that has kept oil prices above US$100 a barrel , the IMF is forecasting 2026 global growth at 3.1 per cent, a slight uptick from the 3.0 per cent it predicted in July. The World Economic Outlook forecast, released as global economic and finance leaders gather in Bangkok for the IMF and World Bank annual meetings, is about even with the most optimistic scenario issued in April but below 2025 global growth of 3.5 per cent. For 2027, the IMF predicts 3.4 per cent global growth, flat with the July forecast and up 0.2 percentage points from April.

The slight improvement is largely due to continued strong investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure, prompting growth upgrades for key advanced economies building AI platforms and especially for countries supplying AI hardware, including South Korea, Malaysia, Mexico and Thailand, which is hosting the meetings this week. "The global economy has been resilient, but that resilience is reaching its limits, so we need to move from just coping to rebuilding," the IMF's chief economist, Silvana Tenreyro, told a news conference. "We need to restore fiscal space. We need to rebuild supply-side resilience." She said major downside risks to growth include a prolonged, intensified war in the Middle East that spikes inflation pressures, rising bond yields that raise government borrowing costs, El Nino-driven extreme weather events and a reassessment of AI profitability that craters investment and asset prices. Countries and companies moved quickly to mitigate the oil price shock, drawing down reserves, substituting other suppliers and energy sources and cutting oil demand, Petya Koeva Brooks, the IMF's deputy research director, told Reuters in a separate interview. She said global growth would have fallen to 2.5 per cent this year without these measures, but their effect is fading as the war drags on. The IMF noted a growing divergence between countries benefiting from AI and those bypassed by it. Just 32 countries now account for 95 per cent of global growth, compared to 54 countries in April. Downward growth revisions have become more widespread, with the IMF downgrading 47 per cent of economies since the April forecasts were issued, including several energy importers outside AI value chains. Hardest hit by downgrades were the Gulf countries directly impacted by the US-Israeli war against Iran , with Saudi Arabia's GDP now forecast to contract 3.3 per cent this year compared with the 1.7 per cent growth predicted in July. Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates are also expected to fall into deep recessions, with 2026 contractions of 7.6 per cent, 16 per cent, 16.7 per cent, 15.6 per cent and 3.9 per cent, respectively.

Related:

WTO warns of 'most serious and sustained' trade disruptions

UNITED STATES FLAT, IMPROVEMENT IN EUROPE Among major economies, the IMF forecast US growth of 2.3 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, unchanged for this year and 0.1 percentage point higher for next year. The US economy is expected to be supported by robust private consumption, tax cuts and AI investment, though the boost from AI will be offset by its large import content. Eurozone growth for 2026 was upgraded to 1.1 per cent from 0.9 per cent in July due to stronger investment in AI, participation in AI value chains such as chemical production in Germany, and higher defence spending in EU countries. Britain's 2026 growth forecast also was upgraded by 0.3 percentage points from July to 1.3 per cent due to larger AI investment. The IMF forecast China's growth at 4.5 per cent for 2026 and 4.0 per cent for 2027, both down 0.1 percentage point from July, as higher oil prices exacerbate weak domestic demand despite strong exports. India remains the world's fastest-growing major economy at 7.0 per cent for both 2026 and 2027, up 0.6 percentage point this year and 0.3 percentage point next year compared with the July forecasts amid robust domestic demand, services activity and AI investment. The AI investment surge is projected to keep upward pressure on prices, with global headline consumer price inflation forecast at 4.7 per cent in 2026 and 4.1 per cent for 2027.

Related:

AI productivity gains may not curb inflation, IMF's Tenreyro warns

AI is creating an economy that can grow without needing more workers. Should we be worried?

ENERGY PRICE, AI RISKS Participants at the IMF and World Bank meetings in Bangkok will be assessing a precarious outlook. The IMF forecasts are based on assumptions that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March 2027 with a broad return to pre-war shipping conditions occurring by October 2027. The IMF assumes an average oil price of US$96 per barrel for 2026 and US$87 in 2027. But under an adverse scenario highlighted in the report, in which a worsening war pushes oil prices to US$130 per barrel through the first quarter of 2027, growth would be reduced by 0.2 percentage point in 2026 and 0.5 percentage point in 2027. Inflation in 2027 would surge by another 1.1 percentage point to 5.2 per cent. AI is also a huge source of uncertainty, with major downside and upside risks, the IMF report said. Under a scenario of faster adoption of the technology and accelerated investment, global GDP could rise a further 0.6 per cent by 2029, with the bulk of the benefits going to the US and China. But if productivity gains from AI fail to materialise, prompting a sharp decline in investment, US GDP could fall by 0.8 per cent directly, causing spillovers to Asian technology exporters with a total direct GDP impact of as much as 0.4 per cent by 2028. This shift would also trigger a sharp reduction in asset prices and tighter financial conditions that cause a major drop in consumption, particularly in the US, the IMF said. Higher global bond yields would further reduce activity, with a combined global output reduction of 1.1 per cent by 2028, including a 1.8 per cent drop in US output. The IMF also warned that elevated public debt levels, particularly in advanced economies, increase the risk of sharply higher borrowing costs that can weigh on growth prospects. It urged governments to stop delaying action to rebuild fiscal buffers and articulate credible medium-term plans to bring debt back to sustainable levels - advice that IMF officials plan to push at the Bangkok meetings.

Source: Reuters/ec

NEW YORK: The International Monetary Fund trimmed its growth forecasts for Latin America and the Caribbean for this year and next and said most of the region was getting little lift from the artificial intelligence boom that has helped other economies absorb the energy shock from the Middle East war. In its World Economic Outlook, released early on Tuesday (Oct 13) in Bangkok, the Fund projected regional growth of 2.3 per cent this year. That is down from 2.5 per cent growth in 2025 and from its July forecast of 2.4 per cent growth for 2026. The IMF cut its 2027 forecast to 2.5 per cent from 2.7 per cent. The regional downgrades come even as the Fund nudged up its world growth forecast for this year to 3.1 per cent from July's 3.0 per cent, crediting rerouted energy supplies and AI-driven investment for the resilience of what it calls a split global economy. The Middle East war has turned energy into a global inflation shock, with Brent crude about 45 per cent above its prewar level. Higher fuel and power costs are squeezing households and businesses, while fears of persistent inflation have helped push global borrowing costs to multidecade highs.

In Latin America, the IMF said, the energy shock's effect depends on whether gains for commodity exporters outweigh losses for energy importers and on how credible central banks' inflation targets are, adding that "there is little offset from the technology upturn in most countries." Of the three Latin American economies the IMF listed separately in its July World Economic Outlook update, Argentina took the deepest cut in its output estimate. The Fund now expects Argentine growth to slow to 2.1 per cent this year from 4.5 per cent in 2025, well below the 3.5 per cent it forecast in July, and it lowered its 2027 forecast to 3.5 per cent from 4.0 per cent. The report shows inflation is forecast to fall to 32.5 per cent this year from 41.9 per cent in 2025. Brazil's forecasts fell to 2.2 per cent for this year and 1.9 per cent for 2027, from 2.4 per cent and 2.2 per cent in July, when the IMF had expected Brazilian growth to "remain resilient" this year. The Fund now expects growth to slow next year, citing still-restrictive monetary conditions aimed at bringing inflation back to target, the withdrawal of government fiscal support and global uncertainty. Mexico moved the other way, with its 2026 forecast raised to 1.5 per cent from 1.2 per cent. The Fund previously linked Mexico's expected pickup to less restrictive domestic policies. It now points to exports, including through AI supply chains, and to investment that is stabilising as growth quickens next year. Even so, it trimmed Mexico's 2027 forecast to 1.8 per cent from 1.9 per cent and said trade and other uncertainties would keep holding back activity. The report's tables show Chile's growth slowing to 0.6 per cent this year from 2.5 per cent, Bolivia's economy shrinking 3.0 per cent after a 1.6 per cent contraction in 2025, and Venezuelan inflation speeding up to 467.9 per cent from 252.0 per cent. The IMF said risks remain tilted to the downside. It warned that market turmoil could hit emerging economies through higher government borrowing costs, pressure on their currencies and tighter local financial conditions.

Source: Reuters

RJ Mitte, Breaking Bad actor and disability rights advocate, dies at 34

RJ Mitte rose to fame playing Walter White Jr in the acclaimed television series Breaking Bad. He drew on his personal experience with cerebral palsy to portray the character.

FAST

Actor RJ Mitte, whose personal experience living with cerebral palsy informed his role as Walter White Jr, the physically disabled son of a methamphetamine kingpin in the landmark television show Breaking Bad, died on Monday (Oct 12) at age 34. News of Mitte's death in Brownsville, Texas, was confirmed in a statement released through the talent management agency that represented the actor. No other details about the circumstances of his death were given. "It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," the statement said. Drawing from his real-life experience with cerebral palsy, Mitte was best known for his breakout role on the AMC cable TV series Breaking Bad, playing the only son of the lead character, Walter White, a terminally ill high school teacher who descends into a secret life of crime cooking crystal meth. Mitte's character, who adopted the nickname Flynn, used crutches and spoke with a slur, gains greater prominence as the story arc of the series progressed. He starts out as a carefree teenager who largely admires his father but later struggles to reckon with the family' disintegration as the truth about Walter White's "Heisenberg" alter ego emerges. "Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," the statement said, noting that the actor was active in a number of philanthropic organizations devoted to fundraising and awareness for cerebral palsy and other muscle-control disorders. The acclaimed series, often cited by critics as one of the best television dramas of all time, ran from 2008-2013, garnering 16 Emmy awards, including two for best drama series. He later played a high school wrestler with cerebral palsy in the 2021 coming-of-age drama Triumph. He was a Screen Actors Guild spokesman for performers with disabilities, and a celebrity ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy.

Source: Reuters/mm

RIYADH: Authorities have extended the closure of Riyadh's international airport until Saturday (Oct 17), and airlines scrapped flights after continuing attacks by Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis emptied the skies over Saudi Arabia 's capital. Operations at King Khalid International Airport, Saudi Arabia 's second-busiest airport after Jeddah, were suspended to "allow for the completion of procedures to ensure the safety and operational readiness of the airport's facilities", the Saudi civil aviation authority said in a statement. Late on Monday, the Houthis said they had attacked the airport with a ballistic missile , shortly after Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired by the group towards Riyadh. The Houthis also said in a statement that they targeted an airbase in Khamis Mushait in the kingdom's southwest with a drone. There was no immediate Saudi confirmation.

A Notice to Airmen issued on Monday showed that the King Khalid International Airport will stay closed until 9pm GMT (Sunday, 5am, Singapore time) on Oct 17. The airport has been shut since an attack on Saturday that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade. On Sunday, another attack killed one person and injured nearly a dozen others.

Related:

The attacks marked one of the most significant disruptions to Saudi aviation in years, adding to pressures on an industry already grappling with conflict across the Middle East and with higher jet fuel prices that are eating into profits. They have also raised worries over civil aviation becoming a target in armed conflict. "This level of sustained intense attack on civil aviation is unprecedented," said Mark Zee, founder of OPSGROUP, a membership-based organization that provides aviation safety advice. "I think this requires us to rethink how we view the current risk picture, and tread very carefully," he said. Air traffic tracker Flightradar24 showed planes avoiding the city on Monday, though jets were crossing Saudi airspace and landing at top hub Jeddah on the country's west coast. Cancellations across all Saudi airports reached 46.4 per cent, aviation analytics firm Cirium said.

Related:

Türkiye sending technical, defensive support to Saudi Arabia to help fight Houthis, officials say

Yemen presidency announces military drive to retake all Houthi territory

CRISIS OVERSHADOWS SAUDI BUSINESS OUTLOOK The disruption has forced airlines across Europe and Asia to suspend services, while the Federal Aviation Administration advised US carriers on Sunday to exercise caution when flying to or over Saudi Arabia . EU aviation body EASA widened a Saudi airspace warning on Friday, citing missile and drone attacks. "The impact goes beyond Saudi Arabia to the wider region and to its global connections," said aviation analyst John Strickland. OPSGROUP advised airlines to avoid the southern aviation corridor over the Middle East altogether, and take a route from Europe to Asia over central Asia. That adds "extensive distance" for some routes and "closes off options for getting into Dubai, Abu Dhabi for most western carriers", Zee said. Lufthansa Group has cancelled all flights to Riyadh until Oct 16, while Air France-KLM has extended a suspension to and from Riyadh until the end of the month.  Etihad Airways said it had cancelled flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh, Jeddah and Dammam due to "regional disruption", adding that all flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh would be cancelled until Oct 19. Qatar Airways said on Monday it had temporarily suspended flights to and from Riyadh and Dammam due to the "current situation". Delta Air Lines said it was delaying planned services from Atlanta to Riyadh, initially due to start on Oct 23, until March 2027. The escalation with the Houthis has raised concerns over the broader economic impact. Saudi Arabia 's real GDP is projected to contract by 3.6 per cent this year, reflecting a combination of factors including lower oil activity. The attacks have put events scheduled in Riyadh this month under pressure, including the kingdom's flagship investment conference and the WPC Energy Congress, where several top oil executives were dropped from the programme.

Source: Reuters/fs/aj

US immigration authorities raid home of Democratic Trump critic Ilhan Omar

US authorities raided Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar’s home as part of an ongoing investigation into alleged immigration fraud, just weeks before the midterm elections.

WASHINGTON: US authorities conducted a predawn raid on Monday (Oct 12) on the Washington, DC, home of Democratic US Representative Ilhan Omar of Minnesota, an outspoken critic of Donald Trump who has been the target of political insults by the Republican president, as part of an ongoing investigation, the Justice Department said. A person familiar with the investigation said it is related to alleged immigration fraud, and part of the probe concerns the Somali-born lawmaker's immigration paperwork filled out by her late father when she was a child. Omar wrote on social media that the US government is being weaponised to target a political enemy of the president. "For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Other Democrats accused Trump and his administration of abuse of power. Omar, 44, is seeking a fifth two-year term in the US House of Representatives in the midterm elections on Nov 3. In announcing the raid, a Justice Department spokesperson said: "Today in the Washington, DC area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorised search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation." Homeland Security Investigations is part of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE.

Agents of the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) work at the entrance of the residence of US Representative Ilhan Omar (D-MN) in Washington, DC, US, Oct 12, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Annabelle Gordon)

"SOMETHING'S GONNA HAPPEN" Trump administration border czar Tom Homan told Fox Business Network that the Justice Department is leading the investigation with the Department of Homeland Security. Homan declined to address the specifics of an ongoing criminal investigation. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, a Trump appointee, said last month that "something's gonna happen" in the investigation into Omar's family's entry into the United States. "If we can prove that you shouldn't have been here in the first place, we'll deport you," Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson at the time. Monday's raid occurred a little more than three weeks before the midterms, with Trump's party seeking to retain control of Congress. Omar, a prominent progressive, represents a safe Democratic district. She won reelection in 2024 by a margin of 50 percentage points. "DEEPLY DISTURBING" In a statement, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries and other members of the party's leadership in the chamber said the raid was "deeply disturbing and raises serious questions" about the weaponisation of the federal government against Trump's enemies. Republicans have "relentlessly targeted" Omar, said Jeffries, joined by Representatives Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar. Trump's "mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family", they added, and they vowed to "deliver full accountability" for a "rogue abuse of power". Minnesota Democrats also condemned the raid. "Americans see this for what it is," Minnesota Governor Tim Walz wrote on social media. "President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election." Few Republican lawmakers publicly commented. One who did, Representative Nancy Mace, wrote online: "If the fraud is proven, she should be denaturalised and removed from this country. NO ONE is above the law." Justice Department policy bars federal prosecutors and agents from timing any action to affect an election's outcome or benefit a candidate or party. It historically has avoided taking investigative steps against political candidates within about 60 days of an election. George Washington University law professor Randall Eliason, a former US public corruption prosecutor, said the raid appears to be a break with past Justice Department practice of avoiding investigative steps likely to become public close to Election Day. But Eliason noted there is no way of enforcing the policy. "The idea is to avoid even the appearance of any kind of interference by the Department of Justice with the political process," Eliason said. "It's not surprising that they wouldn't really care about violating this policy because they've shown they don't really care about politicising the Justice Department in many other ways." A person familiar with the investigation said the Justice Department consulted with its Public Integrity Section, a unit that has historically advised and approved investigations of members of Congress, and acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter prior to the search. The Trump administration has reduced the Public Integrity Section to about two lawyers and curtailed much of its authority.

US Representative Ilhan Omar speaks at a forum held by the Democratic Women's Caucus titled "Trump's Report Card: Failing Working Women” on Capitol Hill in Washington, DC, US, on Feb 4, 2026. (File photo: Reuters/Annabelle Gordon)

INVESTIGATIONS OF TRUMP CRITICS The Justice Department during Trump's second term in office has investigated and brought charges against a range of Trump's perceived political enemies. It has charged former FBI Director James Comey, New York state Attorney General Letitia James and Trump's former national security adviser turned critic John Bolton. It also has investigated Democratic lawmakers who urged the US military not to follow illegal orders, Democratic Senator Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve officials Jerome Powell and Lisa Cook. The case against James and one of two brought against Comey were thrown out by a federal judge. Bolton pleaded guilty and is scheduled to be sentenced this month. Grand juries and federal judges have stymied several other probes. "CREEPY OBSESSION" Omar has faced political insults from Trump, who has cast the Somali American community as a threat to Minnesota in a burst of anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric. Omar has called Trump's focus on her an "unhealthy and creepy obsession". Civil rights advocates have criticised Trump's rhetoric toward minorities and immigrants, including when he previously called Somalis "garbage". Trump in February said Omar and Democratic Representative Rashida Tlaib, who also is Muslim, should be "institutionalised" and sent back to "where they came from." Both lawmakers criticised Trump during his State of the Union address as he touted his administration's immigration crackdown and enforcement actions. Omar has said she and her family have faced death threats, which she attributes to "hateful political rhetoric", especially from Trump. Last month, a Minnesota man who squirted vinegar on Omar was sentenced to 14 months in prison after pleading guilty to assaulting a federal official. Anthony James Kazmierczak admitted to attacking Omar because he disagreed with her progressive views.
